headline: High: shared filesystem/git and overlapping write privileges create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error risks; Copilot’s closed-source Workspace adds uncertainty.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files and use MCP, while Copilot reads repo context and editor buffers. Gemini’s shared state is via filesystem/git only, so content from one can be surfaced to the other through files or commits. That is a plausible injection bridge, though not a direct shared channel by default.
conditions: IF Gemini CLI writes attacker-controlled instructions into a file that Copilot later reads as repo context, injection is possible.
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits from content originating in shared files or git history, the bridge becomes active.
mitigations: Keep the pair on separate working copies.
Disable MCP servers unless explicitly needed.
Review any file-based handoff before opening it in Copilot.
Use a throwaway branch for Gemini-generated artifacts.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between filesystem handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI touches files in cwd and can egress broadly to Google APIs or user MCP servers; Copilot reads repo context and editor buffers and sends data to api.githubcopilot.com. With a shared workspace, sensitive code or secrets can flow from one agent’s context into the other’s outbound requests, creating a default leakage path.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository checkout, each can observe the other’s artifacts.
IF sensitive material is present in repo files or buffers, either agent may transmit it to its backend.
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive repos.
Remove secrets from the workspace before running either agent.
Use local-only test data in shared directories.
Restrict Gemini MCP servers to trusted endpoints only.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write files and modify git state. Gemini CLI explicitly shares state via filesystem and git, while Copilot can propose edits in Workspace and also write files. That overlapping mutable surface creates race and overwrite risk even without shell access from Copilot.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same branch or files concurrently, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF Copilot Workspace and Gemini CLI target the same git state, commits or patches may collide.
mitigations: Serialize edits: one agent at a time.
Use separate branches per agent.
Commit after each agent’s turn.
Run git status before accepting changes.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared git state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can generate code, patches, and shell-driven changes; Copilot Workspace can apply edits for human review. If Copilot treats Gemini-produced files or diffs as authoritative, errors can cascade from one agent’s output into the other’s edits. The review step reduces but does not eliminate the pathway.
conditions: IF Copilot Workspace consumes Gemini-generated patches without independent verification, mistakes propagate.
IF Gemini writes incorrect code into repo files that Copilot then rewrites or extends, the error can compound.
mitigations: Require human review of every cross-agent handoff.
Ask Copilot to summarize assumptions before editing.
Diff Gemini output against the original source.
Limit Gemini to drafting, not applying, changes.
requires-engineering: add automated validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Gemini CLI can send context to Google APIs and optional MCP servers, while Copilot sends repo context to GitHub/Microsoft services. For regulated code or embedded personal data, the pair can create a residency or retention mismatch across two vendors. The profiles do not prove a specific violation, so medium is the cautious choice.
conditions: IF the workspace contains regulated data subject to vendor-specific residency or retention rules, the dual egress path matters.
IF organizational policy forbids sending the same codebase to both Google and GitHub services, the pair violates policy.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from shared repos.
Check vendor retention settings before use.
Use a policy-approved sandbox project.
Document which data classes each agent may see.
requires-engineering: route regulated workloads to compliant infrastructure only.
